traveler: Pierre Bourlémont (Pierre II, sire de Bourlémont)
title: The Troubadour Cousin: From the Meuse to Ganja to Greccio
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, Frebécourt, above the Meuse
stops.campa: Pierre is born in the castle on its lone promontory above the meeting of the Meuse and the Saônelle, the stronghold the bishops of Toul raised and the Brixey lords made their name. His father is Simon, his mother Agnès; the family of Domrémy and the Vosges estate hold lands across France that yield wine, wool and cotton. From the ramparts the valley runs north toward Greux and Domrémy, the villages the house shepherds. In the halls below, music, song and the love-poetry of the troubadours already fill the evenings.
suggested_refs: Château de Bourlémont at Frebécourt, still standing above the Meuse (monument historique PA00107169)

stops.name: Domrémy: the church of Saint-Rémy, the family's village
stops.campa: The boy rides down the valley with his father to Domrémy, where the lords of Bourlémont hold half the village, the church side bounded by the brook. He hears the bell of Saint-Rémy over the roofs and watches the villagers bring their rents of grain and geese. These are his people and this is his ground: the parish whose children his house will shepherd for two centuries more, until a girl of this same street, born the year the male line fails, speaks the name Bourlémont before her judges at Rouen.
suggested_refs: The parish church of Saint-Rémy at Domrémy, beside the house where Joan of Arc will be born
sources: bourlemont_roster.md (the 1334 aveu: the forte maison of Domremy and half that village)

stops.name: The beech on the Vaucouleurs road, l'Arbre des Dames
stops.campa: On the hillside where the family lands run toward the Bois Chenu stands the great beech the country calls the Ladies' Tree, with its spring running from the ground beside it. Pierre plays beneath it with the village children, and the old wives already tell the romance of the tree: that a Seigneur Pierre de Bourlémont and a lady called Fée once met and loved beneath these boughs. He carries the name of that lord of the story. The fairies keep the tree; the children dance; the water heals the fevered who believe.
suggested_refs: Joan of Arc's trial testimony, 24 February 1431: the Fairy Tree 'belongs to the Seigneur Pierre de Bourlement, Knight'

stops.name: Neufchâteau, the fairs of the Meuse
stops.campa: At Neufchâteau, the walled market town an hour's ride south of the castle, Pierre learns the family trade at his father's side: the wool of the Vosges flocks weighed and bargained, the wine of the southern estates rolled off the carts, letters from the Provence cousins read aloud among the bales. Cloth is the house's second dominion, the loom its second sword. The boy watches silver change hands and learns that a bolt of good cloth travels farther than a knight, and that the roads of trade are also the roads of diplomacy.
suggested_refs: The old market squares of Neufchâteau, where the Bourlémont dead of the last generation will lie with the Franciscans

stops.name: Tarascon, the finca of the Provence branch
stops.campa: Pierre comes south with his father to the finca of the Bourlémont of Provence, the branch of the family grown wealthy in the cloth trade beside the Rhône. Here the salons are never silent: music, singing and the amorous poetry of the troubadours fill every hall of the estate, as they fill all the family haciendas of Provençal culture. And here is his cousin Giovanna, quick-eyed and quicker-tongued, who loves the songs best of all. The two cousins are close from the first summer; the halls belong to them.
suggested_refs: The Tarascon tradition of Pica's Provençal home, carried by the parish memory of Beaucaire and Tarascon
sources: pica_dossier.md (Layer 3, the Tarascon anchor, taken on faith)

stops.name: Beaucaire, the fair across the Rhône
stops.campa: For the feast of the Magdalene the cousins cross the Rhône to the great fair of Beaucaire, where the cloth of Provence meets the merchants of Genoa, Marseille and the Italian towns. Pierre walks the stalls with Giovanna, naming the weaves and the dyes as his father taught him at Neufchâteau; she names the singers. The fair is a whole world laid out on trestles: silks, wool, spice, songs in four languages, and among the Italian cloth-men who come year after year are the traders of Assisi. The river carries everything toward everything.
suggested_refs: The Foire de Beaucaire on the Rhône, the fair that binds Provence cloth to the Italian merchants
sources: pica_dossier.md (Layer 3: the Beaucaire fairs explaining the Bernardone match)

stops.name: Marseille, embarkation with his father
stops.campa: In spring the mission begins: Pierre's father takes ship at Marseille on an errand of commerce and diplomacy that will carry them to the Caucasus, and the boy goes with him. Bales of Provence cloth are swung aboard as gifts and as samples; letters of credit and letters of courtesy travel in the same casket. Pierre stands at the rail as the Vieux Port opens onto the sea, a child of the Meuse learning the salt of the world. The journey east will make him; he will spend his manhood trying to give it away.
suggested_refs: The Vieux Port of Marseille, gate of the Levant trade

stops.name: Constantinople, the Golden Horn
stops.campa: The ship passes under the walls of Constantinople and into the Golden Horn, and Pierre sees the greatest city of the world stacked in gold and smoke above the water. In the quarters of the Latin merchants his father trades cloth and gathers intelligence for the road ahead; the boy gapes at Haghia Sophia and at emperors carved in porphyry. Here the West thins out and the East begins: caravans, interpreters, coins with unreadable faces. He learns his first words of Greek and his first lesson of diplomacy: listen longer than you speak.
suggested_refs: Hagia Sophia above the Golden Horn
sources: the medieval Levant road to the Caucasus (traditional route)

stops.name: Trebizond, the gate of the mountain roads
stops.campa: From the Black Sea the travelers land at Trebizond, where the mountains stand up behind the town and the caravan roads climb toward Armenia, Georgia and the lands of the Kura. The cloth is loaded onto mules; the sea-legs are traded for saddle-sores. Pierre rides among drovers and monks and silk-men, hearing the languages change at every pass. His father tells him the names of the kingdoms ahead and the courtesies each expects. The boy keeps a wooden tablet of new words, the first cipher of his life.
suggested_refs: The Black Sea walls of Trebizond, head of the caravan road to the Caucasus

stops.name: Tiflis, the Kura road into Arran
stops.campa: The caravan comes down to Tiflis on the Kura, where the Georgian kingdom glitters between the mountains and the baths steam under the fortress. Pierre's father pays the courtesies of a passing envoy; the boy watches falcons flown from gloved fists and hears psalms sung in a tongue older than Latin. Then the road bends southeast, following the great river down into Arran, the country of orchards and silk between the Kura and the Araxes. Somewhere ahead, in a city of poets, an old master is waiting whom neither of them has heard named.
suggested_refs: The Narikala fortress above the Kura at Tbilisi
sources: the Kura valley road to Ganja (traditional)

stops.name: Ganja, arrival at the court
stops.campa: Father and son ride into Ganja on the Ganjachay, the city of gardens and poets in the country of Arran, and are received at court on their errand of commerce and diplomacy. The bales of Provence cloth are unrolled before connoisseurs of silk; the letters of courtesy are read; the mission is welcomed for the winter. Pierre, a French boy in a Persian court, is a wonder to the courtiers and they to him. In this city lives Nizami, the poet who never leaves it, whose verses the whole East carries away instead.
suggested_refs: The Nizami Ganjavi Mausoleum outside Ganja

stops.name: Ganja: Nizami takes a liking to the young Frank
stops.campa: Nizami likes Pierre Bourlémont. The master who refuses every sultan's invitation makes room at his side for a merchant's boy from France, and through the winter they read together the stories of the Shahnameh of Ferdowsi: the Age of Heroes, kings and paladins and the long war of Iran and Turan. The poet unrolls the verses; an interpreter carries them across; the boy leans in until he needs the interpreter less. What passes between them is not trade and not diplomacy but the third thing both serve: the story that outlives the road.
suggested_refs: Illuminated Shahnameh manuscripts of the Age of Heroes

stops.name: Ganja, the tragedy of Rostam and Sohrab
stops.campa: Nizami tells the boy the great tragedy: how Rostam, mightiest of the heroes, met in single combat a young champion of Turan and killed him, and only as the boy lay dying saw his own clasp on the young man's arm and knew he had slain Sohrab, his son. Pierre weeps at the telling. The old poet lets him weep, and then says that grief is also an inheritance, and that a father and a son who travel together are spared nothing except not knowing one another. Pierre never forgets it; one day he will hold his own son's hand in a cave in Italy.
suggested_refs: 'Rostam mourns Sohrab', the Shahnameh miniature tradition

stops.name: Ganja, Bijan's cipher
stops.campa: Next the poet tells of Bijan of the suffering heart, of Rostam's line, imprisoned in the pit for the love of Manijeh, and of the mode of cipher he used, secret messages sent to his grandfather so that rescue could ride without the enemy reading it. Pierre, keeper of a boy's word-tablet, is enchanted: love has a code, and the code is love's servant. He begins devising ciphers of his own in the margins, French words in Persian dress. The lesson seeds everything after: that the deepest messages travel hidden, knotted, sub rosa, and are read only by the beloved.
suggested_refs: 'Bijan in the pit', the Shahnameh miniature tradition

stops.name: Ganja, Zal's serenade beneath Rudaba's wall
stops.campa: In the deep of winter Nizami tells the sweetest story: Zal of Rostam's house serenading at the castle wall of his love Rudaba. Because his words were sweet, she let down her long hair for him to climb to her. Pierre learns the whole scene by heart: the voice below the wall, the tower, the black rope of hair. He begins to understand what a troubadour is for: song is a ladder, and the sweetness of the words is the strength of the rungs. In the halls of Provence he will climb by this ladder for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: 'Rudaba lets down her hair to Zal', the Shahnameh miniature tradition

stops.name: Ganja, the Azhdaha dragons
stops.campa: Above all Pierre loves the stories of the Azhdaha, the serpent-dragons. These giant monsters travel by land, sea and air; they swallow horses and knights whole; their blood is poison and only superhuman heroes like Rostam can kill them. To eat their hearts makes a man brave enough to conquer kingdoms. To bury their heads in the ground makes the soil fertile for a thousand years. And most important of all, Nizami says it slowly, watching the boy: to wear the skin of an Azhdaha as a tunic can cure the most devastating emotional wounds that make a heart suffer.
suggested_refs: 'Bahram Gur slays the dragon', the great Shahnameh dragon miniatures

stops.name: Ganja: farewell, the poems packed among the bales
stops.campa: At the spring equinox, the new year of the Persians, the mission ends and the caravan forms for the west. Into Pierre's baggage, wrapped like cloth among the cloth, go poems in Persian: the gift of the court and of the master, the beautiful suffering that Nizami's voice intoned all winter. The old poet blesses the young Frank on the road. Pierre carries away the heroes, the ciphers, the serenade, the dragons, and a five-fold philosophy of love's suffering that he does not yet know he will spend in a single summer, on a single cousin.
suggested_refs: Khamsa of Nizami manuscripts, the five poems bound as one

stops.name: Constantinople, the return passage
stops.campa: The road home runs back through Constantinople, and the boy who gaped at the city a year ago walks it now like a small ambassador, greeting merchants by name. In the hostels of the Latins his father settles the accounts of the mission; Pierre sits apart with the Persian scrolls, sounding out the verses so as not to lose the music of them before Provence. He has gone east a child and returns something else: a carrier. The cargo that matters is not in the bales. It rhymes.
suggested_refs: The Latin merchant quarters of the Golden Horn

stops.name: Tarascon: the gift of the Persian poems, the coining of PICA
stops.campa: When Pierre returns to Provence he goes straight to his cousin. He gives Giovanna the poetry in Persian, the stories of the court of Ganja, and the beautiful suffering that the voice of Nizami intoned. She seizes on the bright things like a magpie taking silver, and Pierre, laughing, plays her the nickname that will outlive them both: PICA, the magpie. The cousins are close as ever; the gift is a whole world folded into scrolls. From this day the name Giovanna keeps house indoors and Pica flies about the salons.
suggested_refs: The magpie, la pica, emblem of the name that entered the Assisi ledgers as Domina Pica
sources: pica_dossier.md (Layer 6: the corpus supplies the mechanism of the name)

stops.name: Tarascon, the halls filled with singing
stops.campa: Pierre sings for Pica, filling the corridors of the Bourlémont finca in Provence, spinning poetry about the ecstasy of suffering in love. Looking into Pica's eyes he recites the lyrics he carried from Ganja: that the lord made hearts to burn and break, that romance is an impossible longing. He explains the philosophy he learned in the courts of the East. The household gathers at the doors to listen. It is the old serenade of Zal beneath the wall, translated into Provençal light: the sweetness of the words is the strength of the ladder.
stops.quote: nuestro lord hizo que los corazones ardieran y se rompieran... el romance es un anhelo imposible
suggested_refs: The troubadour halls of Provence, the culture the essays name as the family's own

stops.name: Tarascon, the first four sufferings and their practices
stops.campa: Pierre teaches Pica the five kinds of suffering in love from the Khamsa of Nizami, each with its practice. First, love unreturned or unknown: shyness is a sin, all love must be professed. Second, impossible love, across seas or centuries; therefore we pilgrimage and travel in the world. Third, love unviable or forbidden, like Layla and Majnun between warring houses; therefore we abstain and fast. Fourth, impotent love, when the power to seize the blessing fails us; he swears with a wink he has never known it, and he is ten; therefore alms, when we have capacity. The syllabus is a self-portrait: singing it is the first practice obeyed.
stops.quote: La timidez es pecado... todo amor debe ser profesado
suggested_refs: Layla and Majnun in the Khamsa manuscript tradition
sources: essays/207_hebraic_knots.md (the five sufferings named as the cord's five loops)

stops.name: Tarascon: la quinta herida, the open heart
stops.campa: Fifth is the deepest mystery. Pierre calls it the quinta herida, the fifth wound, the open heart: when we love God and God returns the love even more, the most beautiful and pathetic tragedy of all begins; therefore prayer. Each time he reaches the refrain 'and so we suffer,' he smiles only for Pica. The song knows its singer: unreturned, for a boy of ten is not counted; forbidden, for they are cousins; impossible, for she is promised and packing for the mountains: precocious, performative, authentic. She receives it to be given away later, knotted into a cord her son will wear against his own five wounds.
stops.quote: la quinta herida... el corazón abierto... por lo que sufrimos
suggested_refs: The five-knotted Franciscan cord, topologically the quipu five-knot

stops.name: Beaucaire, Pietro di Bernardone at the fair
stops.campa: At the summer fair of Beaucaire the Italian cloth merchant Pietro di Bernardone of Assisi trades with the Bourlémont of Provence, and the match is made: Pica will marry him and go to Italy. Pierre walks the fair a last time with his cousin, between the stalls where he once named the dyes for her. The magpie is to be carried across the Alps in a merchant's train. He does not grudge the man his fortune; he has already given Pica the dowry that matters: the poems, the court of Ganja, the five sufferings and their practices.
suggested_refs: The Foire de Beaucaire, where the Provence tradition weds Pica to the Assisi cloth trade
sources: pica_dossier.md (Layer 3: the Beaucaire-fair mechanism, on faith)

stops.name: Tarascon, Pica's departure for Assisi
stops.campa: Pica leaves the finca for Assisi to marry Pietro di Bernardone, and she carries away with her the love of music, the spirit, and the fascination with the ecstasy of romantic suffering that her cousin sang into her. The halls of the estate are suddenly very large. Pierre rides with the train as far as the river and watches the barges go. What he gave her will not stay in Italy either: it will pass to a son, be worn as a cord, be preached to birds, be carried back east to the Sultan. The magpie flies with the silver.
suggested_refs: The road from the Rhône to Assisi, the cloth route of the Bernardone

stops.name: Tarascon, word of a son: Giovanni, renamed Frances
stops.campa: Word travels the cloth roads to Provence: in 1181, while Pietro was away in France on trade, Pica bore a son. She dreamed the boy would become a leader and baptized him Giovanni in honor of John the Baptist, and she is raising him in music, lyric song, the voice of nature, Latin and Provençal. When Pietro returned he named the boy Frances: in honor of the French culture of his mother, the romantic poetry of the troubadour, the exquisite cloth of Provence, and the family Bourlémont. Pierre hears his own gift ring in every syllable of the new name.
suggested_refs: The font of San Rufino at Assisi, where the child Giovanni was baptized

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont: sub rosa, the treatise of love
stops.campa: In the year the chaplain Andreas Capellanus writes his treatise De Amore, the book reaches the halls of Bourlémont, and Pierre reads of young Walter, soldier of love, whose amorous attachment is a wound he suffers. The value of secrecy is central: the most ennobling love is clandestine, and operates under the erotic principles of the rose. Pierre, who learned Bijan's cipher at Ganja, recognizes the doctrine at once. He hangs a single red rose above the hall where the songs are sung: what is spoken beneath it is spoken sub rosa, sealed, amplified by the veil.
suggested_refs: Andreas Capellanus, De Amore (1190), the treatise of the wounded soldier of love

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, sire de Bourlémont
stops.campa: Pierre's father Simon dies, and Pierre becomes sire de Bourlémont, lord of the castle above the Meuse and of Greux and Domrémy below it. The traveler now keeps the tower he was born in; the boy who carried poems among the bales now weighs the rents of two villages and the homage of the marches. But the lordship sings. The halls of the Meuse learn the melodies of the Rhône and of the Ganjachay, and the children of Domrémy, dancing at the beech tree, dance on the land of a lord who believes their fairies have colleagues in Persia.
suggested_refs: The keep of Bourlémont, rebuilt by his son's generation after the Holy Land
sources: bourlemont_roster.md (Gen. 3–4: Simon II †1197; Pierre II succeeds)

stops.name: Joinville, the marriage to Félicité de Joinville
stops.campa: At Joinville on the Marne, Pierre weds Félicité de Joinville: the first tie between his house and the great family of the seneschals of Champagne. The match is trade and diplomacy of the oldest kind, but Pierre courts her as a troubadour, all the same: the profession of love aloud, since shyness is a sin; the songs at the wall. To the halls of Bourlémont comes a lady of the Marne with a dowry of alliances, and the two rivers of his boyhood, Meuse and Rhône, are joined by a third.
suggested_refs: The castle of the sires de Joinville on the Marne, house of the chronicler-seneschal to come
sources: bourlemont_roster.md (Gen. 4: ∞ Félicité de Joinville, c. 1185–†1240, the first Joinville tie)

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, word from Assisi: the renunciation
stops.campa: Word comes north on the cloth roads: Pica's son has renounced his inheritance before the bishop of Assisi, stripped himself of his clothes, his father's wealth and the very name Bernardone, and stood naked bearing his broken heart in full humility. And Pica consoled him: we have the same name; I am Giovanna and you are Giovanni; we are John, Joan, Jeanne and Juana; we share the fire of poets, bards and troubadours; you are always my son and a Bourlémont. Pierre, reading, knows the fire she means. He lit it, singing, in a hall in Provence.
suggested_refs: The renunciation before Bishop Guido, the scene at the bishop's palace of Assisi

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, the birth of Joffrey
stops.campa: Félicité bears Pierre his only son, and they name him Joffrey. He is born into a tide of spiritual energy centered on the power of youth that is rising across France; within a year the boy-shepherd Stephen of Cloyes will raise his Children's Crusade, and Joffrey will grow up on the stories, dreaming of leading pilgrims under the banner of the rose cross. Pierre holds the infant on the ramparts and shows him the valley: Domrémy, the beech, the roads. A father and a son who travel together, Nizami said, are spared nothing except not knowing one another.
suggested_refs: The Children's Crusade of Stephen of Cloyes, the tide Joffrey was born into

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont: the Pope kisses the friar's feet
stops.campa: More word from Italy, told at the hearth with the baby Joffrey listening before he can understand: Pica's son, through his dedication to poverty and service, has gathered a brotherhood, and his weakness grew so powerful that Pope Innocent III called him to Rome, bowed, kissed his bare feet, and signed an official order for his order. Pierre laughs until he weeps. The fifth suffering, to love God and be loved back even more, has found its practitioner, and the practice of the fourth, alms, has been turned inside out: the beggar is the richest man in Italy.
suggested_refs: Giotto's Dream of Innocent III and the approval of the Rule, Upper Basilica of Assisi

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont: setting out with Joffrey, twelve years old
stops.campa: When Joffrey turns twelve, Pierre takes his only son to Italy. He hopes the experience will be as formative as his own journey with his father to the Caucasus was; the symmetry is deliberate, a rite of the house. Both of them are curious to meet the dirty friar, and Pierre feels it is important that Joffrey know his older cousin and profit from the connection in his eventual crusade. The baggage is light: cloth for gifts, the old Persian scrolls, a boy's new cipher-tablet. Father and son ride south from the Meuse as the leaves turn.
suggested_refs: The Meuse road south from Bourlémont, the rite of the fathers of the house

stops.name: Tarascon, the halls where he sang for Pica
stops.campa: The road to Italy bends through Provence, and Pierre shows his son the finca of the cloth branch: the corridors he filled with singing forty years ago, the hall where a red rose hung, the river the magpie flew across. He tells Joffrey the five sufferings as they walk the empty salons: profession, pilgrimage, fast, alms, prayer, the way Nizami told him the dragons, slowly, watching the boy. The second suffering is the traveler's own: longing across the extension of space and time. That is why we pilgrimage, he says, and they ride on east.
suggested_refs: The Bourlémont finca of the Provence tradition, keeper of the troubadour halls

stops.name: Greccio, arrival on Christmas Eve
stops.campa: Father and son arrive at Greccio on Christmas Eve, the mountain hamlet above the Rieti valley where the friar cousin keeps this Nativity. The village is full of torches climbing the dark hillside; the friars sing; the whole valley seems to be walking toward one cave. Pierre and Joffrey take lodging among the pilgrims. Somewhere above them in the rock is the man whose naming Pierre heard ring with his own gift: Giovanni who became Frances for the honor of the cloth, the troubadour poetry and the family Bourlémont. Tomorrow they will greet him as kin.
suggested_refs: The Santuario del Presepe at Greccio, the cave of the first nativity

stops.name: Greccio, communion from the friar cousin
stops.campa: In the morning Pierre and Joffrey receive communion from the hands of the friar Bourlémont himself: Pica's son, their own blood. The wafer passes from the scarred hands of the poor man of Assisi to the lord of the fairy tree and his boy. No cloth, no silver, no letters of credit: this is the family trade transacted at last in its true currency. Pierre watches his son take the host from the friar's fingers and feels the generations close like a clasp: the gift he sang into Pica in Provence returned to his own child as sacrament.
suggested_refs: The rock chapel of Greccio where the Christmas mass was sung over the manger

stops.name: Greccio, the cave of the first nativity
stops.campa: That night they visit the cave where the cousin has made a beautiful recreation of the Christmas manger: many lanterns lighting the scene, an ox and an ass, men costumed as magi from far lands, a Virgin and a Joseph, and among the piles of golden hay the child of Bethlehem. Joffrey is struck by the poverty of his Lord's birthplace, seen with his own eyes. Pierre is pleased that the magi resemble those he saw with Nizami: the stories he told Pica now embodied as art and faith. He holds his son's hand while waves of heat emanate from his frail cousin at prayer before the scene.
suggested_refs: Giotto, 'The Institution of the Crib at Greccio', Upper Basilica of Assisi
sources: essays/207_hebraic_knots.md (the magi kings in Phrygian hats at Greccio)

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, the tale at the hearth
stops.campa: Home on the Meuse, Pierre tells the household what they saw: the cave, the lanterns, the golden hay, the magi like Ganja's own, the heat that came off the praying friar like a forge. Joffrey tells it better: the boy has caught fire, and speaks already of the Holy Land, of pilgrims and banners. Pierre lets him burn. He himself has begun to feel the years; he sings less, and when he does it is the fifth suffering more than the first four. The dragons of the forest, he tells the children at the beech tree, are cousins of the Azhdaha.
suggested_refs: The fairy tree of Bourlémont, where Joffrey will one day build the well and the tower

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, word of the seraph of La Verna
stops.campa: Word comes over the Alps that on a mountain of Tuscany the friar cousin has received the five wounds of the Lord from a seraph of fire. Pierre goes very still when he hears it. Five sufferings, he taught Pica; five wounds, the seraph gave her son; the count is exact and the arithmetic is not his: it belongs to the open heart, la quinta herida, loving God and being loved back even more. He remembers the Azhdaha whose skin cures the wounds of the heart, and understands at last that his cousin's son wears no skin at all: the wound itself is the cure.
suggested_refs: The stigmata chapel of La Verna, the mountain given to the brotherhood
sources: essays/207_hebraic_knots.md (the five wounds of La Verna and the Khamsa's five sufferings)

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, the death of Pierre
stops.campa: In the same season that the friar dies singing at Assisi, Pierre Bourlémont dies in his castle above the Meuse, and the two cousins' deaths fold into one autumn. Joffrey, fifteen, holds his father's hand as his father once held his: the clasp of Rostam and Sohrab worn the right way round, father known to son and son to father. At the end Pierre asks for the old Persian scrolls, and for a plain cord knotted with five loops. Each loop a suffering, each suffering a practice: profession, pilgrimage, fast, alms, prayer. On the last one he smiles, as he only ever smiled for Pica.
suggested_refs: The five-looped knot of the Franciscan cord, topologically the quipu five-knot

stops.name: Abbaye de Mureau, the burial among the Prémontrés
stops.campa: They carry the lord of Bourlémont through the woods to the white canons of Mureau, the family's abbey in its fold of the hills, and bury him with the Persian scrolls sealed in the wall of the choir, sub rosa, the way the deepest messages travel. Joffrey stands at the grave already wearing the road east in his eyes; in twenty-two years he will sign his charter to this same abbey for the souls of his house, lord of Domrémy and Greux, home from Jerusalem. The children still dance at the beech tree. The song Pierre carried from Ganja is now in the ground of the Meuse, waiting.
suggested_refs: Joffroy de Bourlémont's charter of 28 May 1248 to the abbey of Mureau, for Domremy and Greux
